generalfeedback.text:
The boundary {@lind(a, b, c)@} crosses the axes at \(({@X@}, 0)\) and \((0, {@Y@})\). [[if test="strictp(rel)"]]The sign is strict, so the line is dashed.[[else]]The sign includes equal to, so the line is solid.[[/if]] Test \((0, 0)\): \(0 {@relt(rel)@} {@c@}\) is [[if test="osat"]]true, so the origin is in \(R\) and the shaded side is the side without the origin.[[else]]false, so the side with the origin is shaded.[[/if]] That is Graph {@cor@}.

Graph {@lw@} shades the wanted side; Graph {@ls@} has the wrong line style; Graph {@lb@} has its crossings swapped.

questiondescription.text:
Linear Inequalities: which graph shows an inequality

Grade 12 CBE Essential 1.3: Choose the graph that shows a linear inequality, with the unwanted side shaded, against graphs with the common errors.

Essential

This question is original to this project.

INNODEMS CBC Grade 12 Mathematics, first draft by Ben Davies, 2026. Aligned to the KICD Senior School Curriculum Design, Essential Mathematics Grade 12 (draft).

truefeedback.text: Graph {@lw@} shades the region where the inequality is true. In this book we shade the unwanted region and leave \(R\) clear.

Graph {@ls@} has a [[if test="strictp(rel)"]]solid line, but the sign does not include the line, so it should be dashed.[[else]]dashed line, but the sign includes the line, so it should be solid.[[/if]]
Graph {@lb@}'s line crosses the axes at \(({@Y@}, 0)\) and \((0, {@X@})\). Put \(y = 0\) and then \(x = 0\) in {@lind(a, b, c)@}.

falsefeedback.text: One graph is correct: check the line's crossings, its style and which side is shaded.
